Typically, this vowel is the last full vowel of the form, i.e. any vowel except /ə/. If the last vowel is /ə/, the preceding full vowel is stressed. A short vowel in word-final position is never stressed. When a word ends in a short vowel, the full vowel immediately preceding it is the stressed one. new_statements.quote: All descriptions of Yuman languages agree that these are stress languages, and that stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word. [...] Uninflected words tend to have stress on the last syllable in direct consequence of the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes. (p. 239) Note that regardless of the complexity of the word, the stress remains fixed on the root. The only thing that can happen to a stressed syllable is that the stress reduces in compound formation to secondary stress on the first member of the compound, thus maintaining the preference for primary stress on the last syllable. (p. 240)

It does not offer a different placement; the only difference is descriptive type (root-based rather than edge-based), and suffixed verb forms such as m-a:ku:xáp-c-ma-yu show that strict fixed: final syllable coding does not h…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per word, fixed on the (typically monosyllabic) root; because Yuman words are built with many derivational prefixes and few, mostly single-consonant, derivational suffixes, uninflected words come out with stress on the last syllable. Diegueno examples: mát 'land', má:t 'body', ák 'bone', xú: 'nose', á: 'go' (p. 239); tə-xə-mə-kwán-p 'is tangled up' with three pre-stress syllables and none after (p. 239). Stress is a bundle of loudness, pitch and length (p. 240). For the Mesa Grande dialect the stressed syllable is typically higher in pitch than the rest, with a less common lower-pitch variant; unstressed syllables have low pitch except a directly pre-stress syllable with a long vowel or a short vowel plus glottal stop (p. 241). Conclusion p. 252: 'Stress is basically morphological, it is a property of the root; length is contrastive.; and pitch is dependent on particular configurations of sequences of syllables in the word and in connected discourse, but has become contrastive in some languages' (Kiliwa, Paipai), not Diegueno.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In compounds the first member's stress reduces to secondary stress, keeping primary stress on the last syllable; this secondary stress 'may also further reduce so as to become indistinguishable from other unstressed material' (p. 240; examples xàtəpá: 'coyote' = xát 'dog' + pá: 'person', màtətáy 'mountain' = mát 'ground' + táy 'big').
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixes 'producing unstressed syllables are common, though they are mostly syntactic in function', so post-stress unstressed syllables occur in verbal constructions with cliticized destressed higher predicates, e.g. m-a:ku:xáp-c-ma-yu 'Are you catching up with him?' (pp. 239-240); footnote 4 (p. 257): some investigators (Redden 1966, Halpern 1946-47) describe suffixes bearing primary stress so that some 'words' have two primary stresses; Langdon treats these as two words. Diegueno has neutralized the short/long vowel contrast in vowel-final roots (p. 241). The stress-shift discussion (pp. 247-253) concerns Mojave only.
new_statements.identity_note: Langdon 1977's Diegueno data are Mesa Grande (p. 241 refers to 'the Mesa Grande dialect in Langdon (1976)'), i.e. Ipai = ipai1240, the same variety as the catalog's deciding source (Langdon 1966/1970). Miller 2001 describes Jamul Tiipay (ISO dih = Glottolog kumi1248, Tipai-Kumeyaay), a sister language, not ipai1240.
